entries.title: One Cold Drink Does Not Mean Always

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: In a fictional cafe, your drink arrived cold. You're writing a review. Which sentence stays close to what you know? First: They never get anything right, and every customer must be disappointed.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Second: On my visit, the drink arrived cold, and that was disappointing. The second sentence still criticises the experience. It doesn't pretend that one visit tells you what happened to every other customer.

entries.prompt: Which sentence describes the experience without claiming to know every visit?
entries.answer: The second. On my visit gives the criticism a clear, honest limit.

entries.title: Your Backup Needs a Decision Time

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: If it rains at noon, we'll change the picnic. I'll confirm the place at eleven. That sounds organised, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: The times don't work together. At eleven, you can't check whether it's raining at noon. Choose a condition you can check before people travel.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Then let's check at ten. I'll confirm the meeting place by ten fifteen, before anyone leaves.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: That's clearer. In this invented plan, the condition and the confirmation time now fit together. We haven't made a weather prediction.

entries.prompt: Should the confirmation come before or after your friends need to leave?
entries.answer: Before they leave. Give people enough time to use the information.

entries.title: An Honest Review Can Explain Who Might Like It
entries.thumbnailHeadline: NOT FOR ME, BUT MAYBE YOU
entries.hook: Your complaint can help someone choose.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Riley tried a fictional cafe while hoping for a quiet conversation. She found loud music and closely packed tables. Her first review said nobody should ever go there. Then she thought about what she actually wanted to tell a reader.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: She changed it to: It was too noisy for our conversation. It may suit you if you want a lively atmosphere. She hasn't withdrawn her complaint.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: She's explained the problem and the kind of visitor who might feel differently. That gives another person useful details for their own choice.

entries.prompt: Has Riley pretended to like the noise, or explained her experience more clearly?
entries.answer: She's explained it more clearly. Her preference and someone else's can both make sense.

entries.title: Change the Plan Without Sending a Puzzle
entries.hook: Your friends shouldn't need the chat history.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Our indoor picnic room isn't available. I'll write: Forget my last message. Everyone can scroll back and work out what I mean.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: They might read only the notification. Send the current plan in one message: The room isn't available. We're moving the picnic to another day, so there's no meeting this afternoon.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: That tells them what changed and whether they should leave home. I don't need to include every idea we considered before deciding.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Right. A complete update can be short. Keep private directions in your actual group chat, and ask the people affected to acknowledge an important change.

entries.prompt: Does forget my last message tell a friend where to go now?
entries.answer: No. State the current arrangement so it makes sense without older messages.
